description: Source-grounded contextual explanations for Moran 1.1.1, Stout 1.1.2 and Papineau 1.1.3; further source detail remains in optional paragraph-adjacent Source Depth.

companions.passage: Russell initially described analysis as finding simpler elements within a complex claim.
companions.title: What does Russell mean by analysis?
companions.explanation: Russell tries to understand a complicated statement by examining its simpler parts and how they fit together. Moran introduces this as an early method of analytic philosophy. Later thinkers change the method, so this is a starting point rather than the definition of the entire tradition.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.simple: Russell tries to understand a complicated statement by examining its simpler parts and how they fit together.
companions.why_here: Moran introduces this as an early method of analytic philosophy. Later thinkers change the method, so this is a starting point rather than the definition of the entire tradition.
companions.remember: Russell: examine the parts of a complex claim.

companions.passage: Singer extends moral consideration to sentient animals, while Parfit asks us to consider
companions.title: Why do future generations matter here?
companions.explanation: Stout connects Parfit's concern for people not yet born with his view of personal identity. Our future selves, on this account, may be psychologically connected to us without being strictly the same person. That makes concern for future interests a wider question than simply protecting one's present self.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: Stout is asking whether our moral choices should count people who have not yet been born.
companions.why_here: This extends the discussion of consequences beyond people alive today.
companions.remember: The future can matter morally.

companions.passage: Hare distinguishes ordinary rule-following from critical calculation; rule-utilitarianism combines a generalization principle with a utilitarian way of selecting rules, though critics question whether it collapses into act-utilitarianism.
companions.title: Why are rules mentioned in utilitarianism?
companions.explanation: Stout explains that Harrod combines two ideas: a Kantian-style reason to follow general rules, and a utilitarian method for deciding which rules would have the best consequences. Utility helps select the rules, but does not by itself explain why we must always act by rules.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: A rule-utilitarian asks which rules generally produce the best results, not only which single act does.
companions.why_here: Stout is examining whether good outcomes alone can explain why we should keep rules.
companions.remember: Rules and single acts are different questions.

companions.passage: while Kantian and phenomenological thinkers continued to ask how an objective world can be known by a subject.
companions.title: What is naturalism doing in this discussion?
companions.explanation: Naturalism looks mainly to nature and the sciences when explaining how things work. Moran contrasts its growing influence with philosophers who also ask how our knowledge can be objective. He is comparing approaches to a shared question, not changing the subject.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.added_value: Resolves the immediate reader question by restating the nearby point in simpler words and showing its role in Moran's current argument. Extra original-source detail lives in the separate optional Source Depth appendix.
companions.simple: Naturalism looks mainly to nature and the sciences when explaining how things work.
companions.why_here: Moran contrasts its growing influence with philosophers who also ask how our knowledge can be objective. He is comparing approaches to a shared question, not changing the subject.
companions.remember: Two approaches; one question about knowledge.

companions.passage: Around 1900, Freud's work,
companions.title: Why does Freud appear among philosophers?
companions.explanation: Moran is pointing to different intellectual beginnings around 1900. Their effects were not all the same. Freud represents a major new way of thinking about the mind, while the other names in this paragraph mark developments in logic and philosophy. This is a historical overview, not a list of one school.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.added_value: Resolves the immediate reader question by restating the nearby point in simpler words and showing its role in Moran's current argument. Extra original-source detail lives in the separate optional Source Depth appendix.
companions.simple: Moran is pointing to different intellectual beginnings around 1900. Their effects were not all the same.
companions.why_here: Freud represents a major new way of thinking about the mind, while the other names in this paragraph mark developments in logic and philosophy. This is a historical overview, not a list of one school.
companions.remember: One period can have several different beginnings.

companions.passage: Husserl opposed psychologism and developed phenomenology as a description of what appears to consciousness.
companions.title: What does phenomenological description mean here?
companions.explanation: Husserl asks us to describe carefully how something appears in conscious experience before forcing it into an explanation. Moran uses this method to show another influential route into questions about knowledge. Husserl and Frege both cared about logic and objectivity, even though their methods developed differently.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.added_value: Resolves the immediate reader question by restating the nearby point in simpler words and showing its role in Moran's current argument. Extra original-source detail lives in the separate optional Source Depth appendix.
companions.simple: Husserl asks us to describe carefully how something appears in conscious experience before forcing it into an explanation.
companions.why_here: Moran uses this method to show another influential route into questions about knowledge. Husserl and Frege both cared about logic and objectivity, even though their methods developed differently.
companions.remember: Husserl: begin by describing experience.

companions.passage: Quine attacked the analytic–synthetic distinction and argued that our beliefs meet experience as an interconnected body, not one statement at a time.
companions.title: Which distinction did Quine challenge?
companions.explanation: The analytic–synthetic distinction separates truths said to depend on meaning from truths said to depend on how the world is. Quine questions whether this neat separation holds. Moran includes him to show that analytic philosophy revised some of its own earlier assumptions.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.added_value: Resolves the immediate reader question by restating the nearby point in simpler words and showing its role in Moran's current argument. Extra original-source detail lives in the separate optional Source Depth appendix.
companions.simple: The analytic–synthetic distinction separates truths said to depend on meaning from truths said to depend on how the world is.
companions.why_here: Quine questions whether this neat separation holds. Moran includes him to show that analytic philosophy revised some of its own earlier assumptions.
companions.remember: Quine challenged a familiar boundary between kinds of truth.

companions.passage: Husserl, Patočka, Derrida, and Habermas debated its intellectual inheritance and the limits of European identity.
companions.text: Europe itself became a philosophical question
companions.title: Why is Europe a philosophical question?
companions.explanation: Here 'Europe' means more than a place on a map. Philosophers also argue about the ideas and traditions associated with it. Moran has been discussing wars, migration and changing intellectual centres. He now asks how that history changes the way philosophers understand Europe's identity.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.added_value: Resolves the immediate reader question by restating the nearby point in simpler words and showing its role in Moran's current argument. Extra original-source detail lives in the separate optional Source Depth appendix.
companions.simple: Here 'Europe' means more than a place on a map. Philosophers also argue about the ideas and traditions associated with it.
companions.why_here: Moran has been discussing wars, migration and changing intellectual centres. He now asks how that history changes the way philosophers understand Europe's identity.
companions.remember: Europe is both a place and a contested intellectual idea.

companions.passage: He proposed testing and revising moral principles through reflection and practice.
companions.title: What does revising a moral principle mean?
companions.explanation: Stout distinguishes a weaker view, where describing and working through a situation shapes which moral questions arise, from a stronger view, where rational experimentation actually makes the outcome good. He is cautious about attributing this stronger anti-realist claim to Dewey himself.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: Dewey treats moral decisions as things we can think through, test in experience and improve.
companions.why_here: Stout is showing an approach that begins with human experience rather than a fixed dictionary definition of good.
companions.remember: Reflection can revise moral judgment.

companions.passage: Stout examines more reductive accounts, including Perry's treatment of value as an object of interest, as well as ideal-observer theories, relativism, and later Cornell realism.
companions.title: Why imagine an ideal observer?
companions.explanation: Roderick Firth proposed interpreting an ethical judgment through how a fully informed, disinterested, consistent observer would respond. Stout uses Moore's challenge to ask why that observer's reaction should settle what I ought to do. Brandt developed a related but differently qualified account.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: The theory asks how someone fully informed and fair-minded would judge an action.
companions.why_here: Stout is reviewing attempts to explain moral judgment through human responses to situations.
companions.remember: The observer is a proposed test, not an actual judge.

companions.passage: Peter Geach also asks how a moral statement can keep its meaning inside an “if … then” argument.
companions.title: Why does an if–then sentence matter?
companions.explanation: Calling stealing wrong may seem like expressing disapproval. But in the statement 'If stealing is wrong, then …,' the speaker is not straightforwardly disapproving of stealing. Geach asks how the expression can still play the same logical role in an argument; Blackburn tried to answer through commitments between attitudes.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: We can use the words 'stealing is wrong' inside an argument without ourselves directly condemning stealing.
companions.why_here: Stout uses this difficulty to test theories that treat moral language mainly as expressing feelings.
companions.remember: Moral sentences also work inside reasoning.

companions.passage: John Mackie's error theory argues that ordinary moral judgments claim an objective authority that the world does not provide.
companions.title: What is an error theory?
companions.explanation: Stout describes two parts of Mackie's challenge. Objective values would be unusual things in the world, and knowing them would require an equally unusual way of detecting them. Mackie therefore held that ordinary moral judgments claim more objectivity than exists and are, strictly speaking, false.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: Mackie thinks ordinary moral judgments claim an objective rightness or wrongness that he says does not exist.
companions.why_here: Stout moves from what moral words do to whether the values they describe are real.
companions.remember: An error theory says the claim to objective value fails.

companions.passage: Sidgwick and Moore appealed to fundamental intuitive principles.
companions.title: Why begin with intuitive principles?
companions.explanation: Stout reports Sidgwick's movement from judgments about particular cases, to intuitive rules, to deeper philosophical principles that cannot themselves be derived from still deeper rules. Stout then asks why these final principles should escape further justification and finds Sidgwick's preference for maximizing good open to challenge.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: Some moral arguments stop at basic principles that are not proved through still more basic rules.
companions.why_here: Stout is asking where justification finally comes from when we judge right and wrong.
companions.remember: Basic principles still need to be understood.

companions.passage: These duties can conflict, leaving particular decisions less than certain.
companions.title: How can duties conflict?
companions.explanation: Ross named duties such as fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, and avoiding harm. Their weight can differ by case, and consequences may be uncertain. Stout emphasizes that recognizing each duty intuitively does not mean that its final priority in a difficult situation is equally obvious.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: You might have a reason to keep a promise and another reason to prevent harm; a real choice may involve both.
companions.why_here: Stout uses Ross to explain why moral judgment cannot always follow one absolute rule.
companions.remember: Several duties may matter at once.

companions.passage: The Prisoners' Dilemma shows why self-interest alone can undermine cooperative rules.
companions.title: Why can cooperation fail?
companions.explanation: Stout's problem is that everyone may be better off under shared rules, yet an individual can gain by breaking a rule while others obey it. If each person reasons that way, the system collapses. Gauthier responds by trying to build commitment into rational agency rather than treating every case as a fresh calculation.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: If everyone breaks a useful rule to gain a personal advantage, everyone may end up worse off.
companions.why_here: Stout uses the dilemma to ask why rational people should stay committed to shared rules.
companions.remember: Immediate gain may harm shared interests.

companions.passage: Scanlon, Rawls, and Habermas developed approaches grounded in agreements that reasonable people could accept.
companions.title: Why do agreements enter moral philosophy?
companions.explanation: Stout distinguishes Scanlon's question about rules no one could reasonably reject, Rawls's imagined agreement behind a veil of ignorance about one's place in society, and Habermas's inclusive discussion in which participants respect each other's viewpoints. All use agreement, but not in the same way.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: These philosophers ask which rules people could accept when they consider one another fairly.
companions.why_here: Stout is comparing another way to justify principles, beyond calculating benefits alone.
companions.remember: Agreement is a way to test justifiable rules.

companions.passage: Frege helped establish the precise logical treatment of statements and meanings.
companions.title: What does Frege contribute to this story?
companions.explanation: Frege used precise logic to study how statements work, including forms that ordinary grammar may hide. Moran identifies this as a major foundation of twentieth-century philosophy. Frege's role here is to show a new tool for questions about language and thought.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.added_value: Resolves the immediate reader question by restating the nearby point in simpler words and showing its role in Moran's current argument. Extra original-source detail lives in the separate optional Source Depth appendix.
companions.simple: Frege used precise logic to study how statements work, including forms that ordinary grammar may hide.
companions.why_here: Moran identifies this as a major foundation of twentieth-century philosophy. Frege's role here is to show a new tool for questions about language and thought.
companions.remember: Frege: clearer tools for logical structure.

companions.passage: The later opposition between analytic and Continental philosophy can obscure their shared origins.
companions.title: Why are analytic and Continental philosophy mentioned together?
companions.explanation: They are names for influential philosophical traditions, but they do not describe two completely separate groups. Moran explains that both faced some of the same older questions. Their later differences make more sense once those shared beginnings are understood.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.added_value: Resolves the immediate reader question by restating the nearby point in simpler words and showing its role in Moran's current argument. Extra original-source detail lives in the separate optional Source Depth appendix.
companions.simple: They are names for influential philosophical traditions, but they do not describe two completely separate groups.
companions.why_here: Moran explains that both faced some of the same older questions. Their later differences make more sense once those shared beginnings are understood.
companions.remember: Different methods can grow from shared questions.

companions.passage: Political philosophy became prominent again through writers such as Arendt and, later, Rawls.
companions.title: Why does political philosophy enter the history?
companions.explanation: Political philosophy asks about questions such as justice, government and how people should live together. Moran is showing how war, persecution and changes in academic life affected what philosophers studied. Political philosophy's growing prominence is part of that historical development.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.added_value: Resolves the immediate reader question by restating the nearby point in simpler words and showing its role in Moran's current argument. Extra original-source detail lives in the separate optional Source Depth appendix.
companions.simple: Political philosophy asks about questions such as justice, government and how people should live together.
companions.why_here: Moran is showing how war, persecution and changes in academic life affected what philosophers studied. Political philosophy's growing prominence is part of that historical development.
companions.remember: Historical events also change philosophical priorities.

companions.passage: Philosophy must also examine its own history: ideas, names, and inherited problems do not have fixed meanings outside the debates that formed them.
companions.text: Philosophy must also examine its own history
companions.title: Why must philosophy study its own past?
companions.explanation: A philosophical idea can be understood differently as later thinkers question or reinterpret it. Moran is warning against a history that simply lists winners, losers and dates. The changing meaning of ideas helps explain why philosophy's development is not one straight line.

source.author: Dermot Moran
source.work: Towards an Assessment of Twentieth-Century Philosophy

companions.added_value: Resolves the immediate reader question by restating the nearby point in simpler words and showing its role in Moran's current argument. Extra original-source detail lives in the separate optional Source Depth appendix.
companions.simple: A philosophical idea can be understood differently as later thinkers question or reinterpret it.
companions.why_here: Moran is warning against a history that simply lists winners, losers and dates. The changing meaning of ideas helps explain why philosophy's development is not one straight line.
companions.remember: Understanding an idea also involves its history.

companions.passage: Stout examines more reductive accounts, including Perry's treatment of value as an object of interest, as well as ideal-observer theories, relativism, and later Cornell realism.
companions.title: What does it mean to value something?
companions.explanation: Westermarck linked wrongness to a person's or community's inclination to disapprove. Perry linked an object's value to someone's taking an interest in it. Stout applies Moore's question to both: does disapproval establish wrongness, or does interest establish goodness? He also notes that Perry later appealed to harmony among interests when discussing overall value.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: Having an interest in something is different from showing that it really is good.
companions.why_here: This returns to Moore's point that identifying things we value is not yet defining goodness.
companions.remember: Being valued and being good are not identical claims.

companions.passage: Stout examines more reductive accounts, including Perry's treatment of value as an object of interest, as well as ideal-observer theories, relativism, and later Cornell realism.
companions.title: Why is relativism included here?
companions.explanation: Brandt connects ethical language to attitudes endorsed after informed, intelligent reflection. Harman interprets moral claims in relation to a community's framework of conventions and attitudes. Stout asks why an informed judge's endorsement, or acceptance within one's own framework, should settle whether an act is really right or wrong. That question remains open for the agent.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: Relativism connects moral judgments with a person's or community's standards.
companions.why_here: Stout asks whether someone's approval or shared conventions can settle what is right.
companions.remember: A standard and its justification are distinct.

companions.passage: The Cornell realists answer that moral properties may be natural, causally important features of reality.
companions.title: What are the Cornell realists claiming?
companions.explanation: Boyd described moral properties as clusters of mutually supporting natural properties, rather than definitions based on one feature. Sturgeon argued that someone's badness or goodness might help explain judgments and actions. Stout asks how the natural cluster connected with a moral term can be shown to coincide with what a person would reach through rational moral reflection.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: They suggest that moral properties can be real features of the natural world.
companions.why_here: Stout sets this against theories that deny objective moral facts and asks how such properties could be recognized.
companions.remember: Realists treat moral truth as about reality.

companions.passage: W. D. Ross instead identified several prima facie duties, such as fidelity, gratitude, justice, and avoiding harm.
companions.title: What is a prima facie duty?
companions.explanation: Stout connects Ross's approach to Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics: autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence and justice. They are distinct considerations that can guide decisions even when no single universal rule determines the answer. This is Stout's example of intuitionism's continuing practical influence.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: It is a genuine reason to act that matters unless other duties in the situation outweigh it.
companions.why_here: Ross helps Stout explain the need to weigh more than one moral consideration.
companions.remember: A duty may count without deciding the whole case.

companions.passage: Stout connects this approach with feminist care ethics, virtue theory, and Continental discussions of our responsibility to others.
companions.text: Continental discussions of our responsibility to others
companions.title: What is responsibility to others here?
companions.explanation: Stout connects Murdoch's attentive moral perception with Buber's 'I–Thou' relation, where another person is not treated merely as an object. For Buber, responding to a particular person also bears on one's relation to God. Levinas develops an ethics of encountering the Other, while Scheler argues that emotional experience can disclose values. These are related approaches, not one identical theory.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: The idea is that another person's situation may call for an attentive moral response.
companions.why_here: Stout connects ethical judgment with how we notice and relate to other people.
companions.remember: Moral attention includes the person before us.

companions.passage: Stout also traces an alternative: Charles Taylor sees self-definition as open to reasoned revision, while existentialists understand radical choice as a deeper source of freedom.
companions.title: What is radical choice?
companions.explanation: Stout contrasts Taylor's rationally revisable self-definition with existentialist radical choice, where value arises from a free decision rather than guiding it from outside. Simone de Beauvoir valued freedom but observed a tension: choosing freely gives a situation meaning, while that settled meaning also limits future freedom. She called this tension ambiguity.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: The existentialist approach stresses a person's freedom in choosing and giving meaning to actions.
companions.why_here: Stout contrasts this with views in which prior reasons guide our choices.
companions.remember: The source of value is part of the disagreement.

companions.passage: Stout traces a shift from pleasure toward preference satisfaction, which influenced decision theory and public policy.
companions.title: Why do preferences matter to utilitarianism?
companions.explanation: Ramsey showed how choices between outcomes could measure preferences and bets could estimate degrees of belief. This helped rational choice and later welfare calculations. Stout nevertheless questions treating preference-satisfaction as the whole of rationality: the fact that people choose what they want does not establish that whatever they want is what they ought to choose.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: An approach based on preferences asks whether people's wishes are fulfilled, rather than measuring pleasure alone.
companions.why_here: Stout follows the change in what counts as a good consequence.
companions.remember: Welfare can be described in more than one way.

companions.passage: Further disagreement concerned whether responsibility requires originating our own causes or having been able to do otherwise.
companions.title: What does originating a cause mean?
companions.explanation: Stout reports Taylor's worry that describing mental events as causes leaves out the agent's own role in acting. Chisholm claimed free will requires some events to be caused by an agent rather than by prior events. Other philosophers judged this metaphysically costly, while compatibilists argued that determinism need not remove freedom or responsibility.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: It asks whether the person is truly the origin of an action, not just one event among earlier causes.
companions.why_here: Stout is comparing different ideas of freedom and responsibility.
companions.remember: Explaining a cause is not yet settling responsibility.

companions.passage: Singer extends moral consideration to sentient animals, while Parfit asks us to consider future generations.
companions.title: What does sentient mean in this argument?
companions.explanation: Stout reports Singer's claim that all and only sentient beings count in overall-happiness calculations. On that principle, if a newborn has less capacity to feel pain than a cow, Singer gives more weight to the cow's well-being in that comparison. Stout also records Singer's qualification that other factors complicate the judgment in practice.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: A sentient being can have experiences such as pain or pleasure.
companions.why_here: Stout explains how Singer decides whose interests count when judging overall welfare.
companions.remember: The criterion is sentience, not species.

companions.passage: rule-utilitarianism combines a generalization principle with a utilitarian way of selecting rules, though critics question whether it collapses into act-utilitarianism.
companions.title: Why might rule-utilitarianism collapse?
companions.explanation: Smart argued that the universally best rule might itself be 'always maximize utility in each case', making rule-utilitarianism collapse into act-utilitarianism. Lyons answered that some formulations escape this collapse, though they may be less plausible on other grounds. Stout presents this as a problem for justifying rules when immediate consequences point the other way.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: If the best rule is simply 'choose the best result every time', the theory no longer differs much from judging each act separately.
companions.why_here: Stout is testing whether rule-utilitarianism can truly justify following general rules.
companions.remember: A rule theory needs a real role for rules.

companions.passage: His open question argument asks: even if something gives pleasure, can we still meaningfully ask whether it is good?
companions.title: Why is Moore's question still open?
companions.explanation: Stout warns that knowing how to use a word does not always mean that its meaning is perfectly clear to us. A question may look open even when it concerns meaning itself. Moore's test must therefore be applied carefully rather than treating every question that sounds discussable as proof that a definition fails.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: Even if something brings pleasure, someone can still ask whether that makes it good.
companions.why_here: Stout begins by separating the meaning of 'good' from descriptions of things called good.
companions.remember: Examples of good things are not definitions of good.

companions.passage: Nozick's experience-machine example questions whether pleasant experience is all we value.
companions.title: What is Nozick's machine meant to test?
companions.explanation: Imagine a machine that could give you every feeling of having achieved what matters to you. You could feel that you had written a great book without actually writing it. If you would refuse the machine, Nozick takes that to suggest that real achievements matter to you, not only the pleasant experience of having them.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: It asks whether feeling happy about achievements is enough when the achievements never really happen.
companions.why_here: Stout is examining whether pleasure alone captures everything we value.
companions.remember: Pleasant experience and actual achievement differ.

companions.passage: Others tried to justify moral rules through self-interest, commitment, or rights.
companions.title: Why move from self-interest to moral rules?
companions.explanation: Baier argued that moral reasons take account of others and override immediate self-interest, while still grounding their priority partly in self-interest; Toulmin appealed instead to harmony among interests. Gauthier argued that rational agency includes commitment, which can sustain cooperation despite a temptation to cheat. Gewirth argued that claiming rights for oneself while refusing others' comparable rights is irrational.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: Following a common rule can benefit everyone even when breaking it seems useful to one person.
companions.why_here: Stout is asking how rational action can include a commitment to other people's interests.
companions.remember: Shared rules need reasons to keep them.

companions.passage: Moral perception joins reason and appropriately developed emotion.
companions.title: What is a thick moral concept?
companions.explanation: Stout reports Philippa Foot's example of the word 'rude'. A person's behavior may meet familiar criteria for being rude, while the word also expresses disapproval. Someone unwilling to make that evaluation may have to decline to use the term itself. This is why a morally thick word cannot be treated as a purely neutral description.
companions.added_value: Clarifies the current concept and its role in Stout's argument; the original additional source discussion is preserved in a nearby optional Source Depth callout.
companions.simple: A word like 'rude' both describes someone's conduct and evaluates it.
companions.why_here: Stout uses this to show that moral understanding may combine attention to facts with an assessment of them.
companions.remember: Description and evaluation can come together.

companions.passage: Scientists observe heated sodium glowing orange and expect it always to do so. Induction moves from finite observations to a universal claim. But past cases cannot logically guarantee future ones.
companions.title: Why is the number of observations a problem?
companions.explanation: The scientist saw only some cases, but the law claims to cover every case. Papineau first asks why those unobserved cases should follow the same rule. Limited evidence, unlimited claim.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: The scientist saw only some cases, but the law claims to cover every case.
companions.why_here: Papineau first asks why those unobserved cases should follow the same rule.
companions.remember: Limited evidence, unlimited claim.

companions.passage: Karl Popper rejects induction as science’s foundation. Scientists propose conjectures, predict and test. One contrary case refutes a universal claim; a theory can survive a test without being proved.
companions.text: a theory can survive a test
companions.title: What does surviving a test mean?
companions.explanation: The prediction succeeded, so this test did not disprove the theory. Popper treats it as an undefeated conjecture, not a proven truth. Survival is not proof.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: The prediction succeeded, so this test did not disprove the theory.
companions.why_here: Popper treats it as an undefeated conjecture, not a proven truth.
companions.remember: Survival is not proof.

companions.passage: Bayesians express belief on a scale from zero to one. Bayesian updating increases confidence when surprising evidence fits a hypothesis. Light bending supported relativity more than ordinary tides, which Newtonian theory also predicts.
companions.title: How does evidence change belief?
companions.explanation: You become more or less confident in a hypothesis when new evidence appears. Papineau introduces degrees of belief to explain positive support for theories. Update confidence as evidence arrives.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: You become more or less confident in a hypothesis when new evidence appears.
companions.why_here: Papineau introduces degrees of belief to explain positive support for theories.
companions.remember: Update confidence as evidence arrives.

companions.passage: Different starting beliefs can converge with enough evidence, but the convergence argument does not explain why a person expecting nature to change tomorrow is irrational.
companions.title: Why do starting beliefs matter?
companions.explanation: Two scientists can begin with different expectations; the same evidence may not settle their disagreement. Papineau asks why some initial expectations count as rational and others do not. The prior needs justification too.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: Two scientists can begin with different expectations; the same evidence may not settle their disagreement.
companions.why_here: Papineau asks why some initial expectations count as rational and others do not.
companions.remember: The prior needs justification too.

companions.passage: The observability problem differs from induction: can evidence justify belief in unseen entities, such as electrons? Realists say indirect evidence can; instrumentalists use theories as calculating tools without accepting their truth.
companions.title: How is this different from induction?
companions.explanation: Induction reaches beyond observed cases; unobservability concerns entities beyond direct sensation. Papineau now asks if indirect evidence can justify beliefs about invisible things. Unseen entity is not the same as untested case.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: Induction reaches beyond observed cases; unobservability concerns entities beyond direct sensation.
companions.why_here: Papineau now asks if indirect evidence can justify beliefs about invisible things.
companions.remember: Unseen entity is not the same as untested case.

companions.passage: Norwood Hanson notes that two astronomers interpret sunrise differently; a physicist sees a particle pair where others see marks. Kuhn and Feyerabend argue that rival theories can lack a shared standard, or be incommensurable.
companions.title: How can the same sunrise be seen differently?
companions.explanation: Our beliefs shape how we understand the sight in front of us. Hanson’s example introduces disagreement about theory-independent observation. Seeing includes interpretation.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: Our beliefs shape how we understand the sight in front of us.
companions.why_here: Hanson’s example introduces disagreement about theory-independent observation.
companions.remember: Seeing includes interpretation.

companions.passage: For Papineau, consistent with the evidence does not mean equally supported by it. One theory may fit the data yet be less plausible than another. This challenges Popper’s demarcation criterion.
companions.title: Why is fitting evidence not enough?
companions.explanation: A theory may avoid contradicting observations yet still be less plausible than another. Papineau uses this difference to answer underdetermination and Popper. Fits is not best supported.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: A theory may avoid contradicting observations yet still be less plausible than another.
companions.why_here: Papineau uses this difference to answer underdetermination and Popper.
companions.remember: Fits is not best supported.

companions.passage: Naturalized epistemology studies science through history, psychology and sociology. A hypothetical prescription says: if you want goal Y, use method X when evidence shows X achieves Y.
companions.title: How does studying science tell us what to do?
companions.explanation: Pick a goal first; then investigate which practices achieve it. This lets a naturalist recommend methods without deriving an ought from a bare is. If goal Y, choose effective method X.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: Pick a goal first; then investigate which practices achieve it.
companions.why_here: This lets a naturalist recommend methods without deriving an ought from a bare is.
companions.remember: If goal Y, choose effective method X.

companions.passage: Defining causal direction by earlier and later becomes circular if time’s order is explained by causes. David Lewis instead uses an event’s multiple future traces, such as fingerprints and recordings.
companions.title: Why not define causes as earlier events?
companions.explanation: If time’s direction is explained through causes, that definition goes in circles. Papineau therefore examines traces and probabilistic relations. Earlier does not automatically mean cause.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: If time’s direction is explained through causes, that definition goes in circles.
companions.why_here: Papineau therefore examines traces and probabilistic relations.
companions.remember: Earlier does not automatically mean cause.

companions.passage: Smoking raises cancer risk without making cancer inevitable. A falling barometer and rain are correlated but share falling air pressure as a cause. This common cause can screen off their association.
companions.title: What gets screened off?
companions.explanation: Once the shared cause is known, the first effect offers no further clue about the second. Papineau uses the barometer and rain to test a probabilistic account of causes. Common cause explains shared effects.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: Once the shared cause is known, the first effect offers no further clue about the second.
companions.why_here: Papineau uses the barometer and rain to test a probabilistic account of causes.
companions.remember: Common cause explains shared effects.

companions.passage: Subjective probability measures belief; objective probability describes chance in nature. Frequency theories use repeated outcomes but struggle with single-case probabilities and hypothetical infinite sequences. Propensity theories take chance as a physical disposition.
companions.title: Why is a single toss difficult for frequency theory?
companions.explanation: One coin toss belongs to different possible groups with different observed rates. Papineau asks how any one group can define the objective chance of that toss. One case; many reference classes.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: One coin toss belongs to different possible groups with different observed rates.
companions.why_here: Papineau asks how any one group can define the objective chance of that toss.
companions.remember: One case; many reference classes.

companions.passage: Historical reduction fails as a universal account because newer theories sometimes replace older ones. Metaphysical reduction asks whether everything is physical. Papineau distinguishes this possibility from reducing every special-science law to physics.
companions.title: What does this kind of reduction ask?
companions.explanation: It asks if higher-level events are ultimately physical, not whether new theories preserve old ones. Papineau distinguishes this from the history of scientific theory change. Physical event need not have one type-law.
companions.added_value: Directly clarifies the immediate argument in Papineau's current paragraph, without opening an unrelated discussion.
companions.simple: It asks if higher-level events are ultimately physical, not whether new theories preserve old ones.
companions.why_here: Papineau distinguishes this from the history of scientific theory change.
companions.remember: Physical event need not have one type-law.
